steps.action:
The first storm of the autumn came in low and quiet, as if it wanted to listen before it spoke.

Elias Cobb stood at the gallery rail of Harrigan Light and watched the horizon blur into a dull smear of slate and pewter. The sky had the color of old tin. Rain whispered more than it fell, but he could see the long line of swell out beyond the reef, and the way the cormorants had abandoned their jagged posts on the black rocks. That told him more than the barometer.

“Right on time,” he said, though there was no one there to hear.

He talked anyway. A man who kept a light and never spoke aloud would start hearing other voices soon enough. Elias preferred his own, so he let it roam.

He checked the lantern room a third time. The lens—her lens, he sometimes thought, as if the glass were something alive—was clean and gleaming, a great Fresnel crown of crystal ribs and prisms taller than he was. The lamp inside, converted to electricity five years back, sat in its brass cradle like something half-holy, faint smell of warm metal and old oil clinging to it no matter how modern they’d tried to make it.

The Coast Guard had sent electricians and inspectors. They’d taken away the old kerosene tins and the boxes of mantles, had replaced the clockworks with a smooth electric drive that turned the lens without the ticking whirr he’d known for thirty-one years. They’d even, in their proud way, suggested that in a few more years Harrigan Light might be automated.

As if the place could run itself. As if the sea would make an exception and behave.

Elias put his palm flat against the outer glass of the lantern room. The wind was only a murmur now, a testing breath. It had been a hot summer. The ocean had steamed and shimmered, the air thick with the sickly-sweet rot of kelp. Now it was emptying itself, breath by breath, about to remember its power.

“You’ll want your light tonight,” he said quietly.

He went down through the hatch and the spiral of iron steps that corkscrewed through the white tower. The steps had a rhythm he knew better than the lines of his own face. There were seventy-two from lantern to watch room, sixty-one from watch room to service room, fifty-eight again to the entry door, and each one with its own chips and scrapes and stains. He could have walked it blindfolded. Sometimes he did, when he woke into old dreams of surf and panic and the sickening thud of hull on reef.

The stones of the tower were cold even in late afternoon. Outside, the air still held a trace of summer, but in here it was always at least one season behind, as if the walls preferred a slower kind of time.

In the service room he checked the backup batteries, the fuel for the emergency generator, the little toolbox that had belonged to his father. It still held the narrow wrench for the old pressure lamps, though there was nothing left here that used it. He couldn’t quite bring himself to move it out.

Everything in order. It usually was. The sea didn’t forgive laziness.

On the shelf by the window sat the logbook, a heavy ledger with cloth corners worn to fuzz. He flipped it open to that day’s page. October 3rd.

1400: Skies overcast, wind ESE 8 kts, vis. 5 nm. Bar. 29.72 and falling. Hazy swell, 4–5 ft. Cormorants left rock. Storm likely by nightfall.

In the column for “Remarks,” he paused. Technically, he was meant to note anything unusual: radio problems, contact with passing ships, maintenance done. Fishing boats he recorded by habit, even though the printed guidelines didn’t require it. Under “Remarks” he wrote, in the same small precise hand he'd used for years:

Fog banks retreat. Odd feeling in air. Like waiting.

He closed the book. Old habit tried to make him add one more line: The sea remembers. But that one he kept for himself.

He boiled water on the cast-iron stove, added two spoons of loose tea to the chipped blue pot, and then, because it was that kind of afternoon, poured a splash from the bottle of cheap whiskey that lived in the cupboard behind the flour tins into his own mug. The drink warmed his hands when he wrapped them around it.

The lighthouse had three rooms and a ghost.

The rooms were simple: service room with its stove and table and cupboards; bunkroom with its narrow metal-frame bed bolted to the wall, a small wardrobe, and a single chair under the round porthole; and the watch room above with the radio, logbook desk, and the ladder up to the light. Under the lowest floor, in the base of the tower, was the oil room where the old tanks had once stood. Now it was storage and echo and cold.

The ghost did not rattle chains or wail. It did not appear as a pale young woman in widow’s black, nor as a drowned sailor dripping weed and seawater. If it had, Elias thought he would almost have been relieved. That would have been easier to classify.

No, the ghost at Harrigan Light was the sound of a bell where no bell was, heard faintly in fog. It was the way the door sometimes shifted open by half an inch when there was no draft. It was the certainty, when he leaned out in a gale to clear a clump of sea-wrack from the lens rail, that a hand he couldn’t see had just brushed the back of his coat to steady him.

And once, thirteen years ago, it had been a voice calling his name from the rocks when no one should have known him there. That had been the only time he had answered aloud: “Anne?” With the wind trying to tear the word from his mouth.

No one had answered back, because no one was alive to.

He had spent a decade afterward convincing himself that the voice had been only wind and spray and the fierce compassion of panic. But every autumn, when the first storm rose, the certainty returned like a tide: the dead kept watch, too.

“Makes us colleagues, I suppose,” he said now to the empty room. “Senior staff, even.”

The kettle whistled. He poured his tea, added condensed milk, stirring until the swirl turned the color of a sandbar at low tide. He took the mug up to the watch room, moving more slowly than he once would have. His left knee twinged at the turn of every step. Old shipwrecks lingered in the body as well as the water.

At the top, he tapped the barometer again, though he knew the habit was meaningless with the electric gauge. The digital numbers glowed a fraction lower than before.

“Down you go,” he murmured. “All right, then.”

He checked the radio. The coastal station crackled with a distant voice listing weather updates and wind shifts. Fishing boats gave their call signs as they headed toward harbor. He recognized several of them by ear: the Marianne Rose, Caleb’s boat; the Sable Star, old Dobkin finally retired and his daughter running her now.

“Breaker’s Point to all small craft,” the radio voice said. “Advising return to shelter. Gale warning in effect from 1800 hours. Seas building to 10–14 feet, wind gusts to 45 knots. Repeat, gale warning in effect…”

Elias leaned back in the chair, sipped his tea, and watched the clouds gather.

From up here, the little harbor town of Harrigan lay folded into the hillside, its houses clinging to the slope as if braced against some invisible push. From the waterline the land climbed quickly: wharves and weathered warehouses, nets drying on fences, then lanes and houses with their white clapboards and peeling paint, then the square spire of St. Brigid’s, and above that the dark smear of the pine woods. A road, not much more than a gray scar, threaded from town to the cliffhead where the lighthouse’s supply path began. It was a labor to walk, and in winter the drifts turned it treacherous.

Elias had walked it weekly for years, until his knee had started to stiffen and the Coast Guard had added a standing order: Harrigan Light supplies by boat only, weather permitting. A younger man came out now and then with crates and gossip and news from the mainland. Elias had not gone farther into town than the harbor pier in three years.

It was easier to stay with the tower, with the routines he knew. Sweep the lens. Wipe the windows. Log the weather. Listen.

The first hiss of real rain came against the glass just as he set his mug down empty. It built in a moment from whisper to patter to a steady, close roar, as if someone had turned the sea inside out and draped it over the air.

He rose, went up the last narrow ladder to the lantern room, and switched on the lamp.

For a heartbeat nothing changed. Then the filament flared invisible in its housing, and the great lens caught the outward-slanting beams and bent them into a focused pillar of white that punched through the dim.

Slowly, grandly, Harrigan Light began its work: four seconds of brightness, two of dark, over and over as the lens turned on its quiet motor. From the town below it would appear as the familiar signature: flash, flash, darkness, flash, flash, darkness. A code that had been burned into Elias’s life as surely as it had into the charts of a hundred captains.

He watched the beam sweep across the gray sea and vanish into the rain, and felt the same small easing in his chest he always did when the light first came up at dusk. As if some muscle he didn’t know he was holding finally relaxed.

“You mind the reef,” he said to the empty horizon. “I’ll mind the light.”

By full dark, the storm had arrived properly.

The tower shuddered at the heavier gusts. Spray reached the gallery windows in tall, angry fingers that slapped and ran, leaving snail-trails of foam. The sound of the surf on the reef had lost its individual crashes; it was a continuous, low roar now, as if the ocean were grinding its teeth.

Elias paced the watch room in a slow, tight circuit, checking the instruments every few minutes though he knew they wouldn’t change much now: wind steady at 40 knots from the east-southeast, gusts to 55. Visibility half a mile. Seas, if the buoy reports could be trusted, fourteen feet and climbing.

He thought of the ships out there, mostly beyond his horizon: the big freighters and container behemoths that paid no mind to a small point of light on an old coast, moving by GPS and satellite and screens glowing green in some distant wheelhouse. The lighthouse was a redundancy to them. A quaint old habit.

But there were still the smaller ones. The coasters. The older trawlers with their rust-streaked hulls and patch-job radars. The men and women who fished because they could not think of anything further inland that felt like living.

Dependable, they had told him, you’ve been. Dependable for thirty-one years, Elias. That’s the word they’d used when the letter came, typed on thick cream paper with the Coast Guard seal at the top. The letter had spoken politely about retirement, about opportunity for new pursuits, about modernization. It had used that word three times.

He had set the letter on the kitchen table, placed his tea mug on top of it, and left it there for three days. When the supply boat came, he tried to hand it back, unsigned.

“Orders, Mr. Cobb,” the young officer had said gently, not taking it. “They’ll send it again if you don’t keep that one.”

He’d signed it that night, the tower cold around him. Forced into neatness by the weight of the thing, he’d written his name so clearly that it looked like a stranger’s.

His last scheduled day was marked in the logbook already, three weeks from now. October 24th. Automate Harrigan Light, the notes in the margin read in another man’s hand. Transfer Keeper Cobb to shore duty, pending.

“Shore duty,” he said aloud now, contempt soft but steady. The storm outside didn’t care for inland words like that.

The radio crackled. He moved to it, adjusted the gain.

“… Breaker’s Point to all stations, be advised—” the dispatcher’s voice came, fuzzy with static. “We have report of—repeat, we have report of missing vessel, the Starling, call sign N-4-1-S. Last contact sixteen-thirty hours, approximately ten nautical miles east of Harrigan Light. Sighting from shore suggests vessel may be off course. All stations in vicinity stand by to assist.”

Elias’s hand tightened on the radio mic.

“Harrigan Light to Breaker’s Point,” he said, pressing the button, voice steady by long habit. “Starling, N-4-1-S, confirm last distance and bearing. Over.”

There was a crackle, a carrier wave hissing. For a moment he thought the signal had cut out; then the dispatcher came back, words faint but intelligible. “Harrigan Light, Breaker’s Point. Confirm last known: ten nautical miles E by SE of your position. Report from shore watch indicates vessel running without proper navigation lights. Possibly power failure. Visibility in that sector one quarter mile. Over.”

“Copy, power failure,” Elias said. “Visibility reduced. Harrigan Light lamp active and rotating. Will monitor and report any visual. Over.”

“Affirmative, Harrigan. Be advised, Coast Guard cutter Venture is en route from south, ETA ninety minutes. Over.”

Ninety minutes. In this weather, in the dark and swell, ninety minutes was a long time to be half-blind near Harrigan Reef.

He pulled a pencil from behind his ear, sketched quick on the pad they kept by the radio: a small crude compass, the tower, a ring for the reef, the mark for ten nautical miles east by southeast. There. That put the Starling right where the swell would be worst once the tide turned, with the reef between her and the open water.

“Could be they swing wide,” he said, though no part of him believed that. In a failure, people didn’t usually manage wide.

He went up to the lantern again.

Outside, the night had thickened into something you could lean on. The rain came in slant lines, driven hard enough now that it bounced off the glass in little bursts like handfuls of thrown gravel. Between gusts, he could see the white combs on the waves, tall and uneven. The reef’s outermost teeth were ghost-pale where the water shattered on them, vanishing and reappearing with every surge.

He stepped out onto the gallery for a better angle, one hand on the rail. The wind slapped at him, trying to grab the breath from his lungs. He narrowed his eyes against the sting of rain and salt.

Far off, beyond the chalky line of the reef, the night seemed uniform. Then, as the beam of the light swept that sector, he saw it: the briefest, faintest wink of redness. Gone as soon as he blinked.

Port running light, starboard dark. No masthead. Power indeed failing, or systems damaged. And the position—he judged by the angle, by long instinct honed through years of watching dots of light move against this particular horizon—too far south, too close in.

He ducked back through the hatch, called down, “Possible visual, bearing one-five-two degrees,” out of habit, though only the stones heard him.

Back at the radio: “Breaker’s Point, Harrigan Light. Intermittent visual on red running light bearing one-five-two degrees, approximate distance eight to ten miles, appears to be closing on reef. No masthead light, no reply to hail. Repeat, no reply. Over.”

“Harrigan, Breaker’s Point copies,” came the response, slower this time, the dispatcher’s calm thinned. “Confirm vessel on collision course with Harrigan Reef? Over.”

“Affirm,” Elias said. There was no room in a storm for softening. “Advise cutter Venture they’ll want to cut in east of the shoals. Suggest additional hails on sixteen, no response here. Over.”

“Understood. Continue visual monitoring and report any change. Breaker’s Point out.”

He returned the microphone to its cradle and tried to ignore the way his hand shook for a moment before he drew it back.

The last time there had been a ship on the reef in a storm like this, he had been younger, strong enough to rope himself to the gallery rail and half-haul, half-slide down the seaweed-slick path to the lower point where the lifeboat could launch. That night the village men had braved the surf, longboat rising and dropping like a splinter on the back of something furious. They had brought six shivering men ashore, one with a broken leg, one clutching a soaked canvas sack as if its contents weighed more than his own life.

“The others?” Elias had asked when they’d staggered up near the base of the tower. The captain—broad-shouldered, his beard full of foam—had only shaken his head once, hard. Behind him, out on the reef, the white hull of the Delilah had angled wrong, already speaking of the sea’s long intentions.

Later, when headlights had swung across the rocks, when someone from town had placed a blanket over Elias’s shoulders and someone else had pressed a flask into his hand, a woman had pushed through the knot of figures and grabbed his arm.

“Was he there?” she’d asked. “Did you see him? Henry Cobb. My brother.”

Only then had Elias realized why the eyes of the rescued captain had seemed so familiar.

Now, in the watch room, he felt the ache in his knee twang ghostlike at the memory of that winter-cold spray. He was older by far. The Coast Guard had its own rescue crews; the harbor had its own modern lifeboats, fast and loud and bright with painted steel.

But the reef had not shifted. The reef cared nothing for new paint or letters of retirement.

“Not yet,” he muttered. “You’re not done with me yet.”

He climbed back to the lantern and studied the darkness. The red wink appeared again, nearer, lurching unevenly between troughs.

“Too fast,” he said under his breath. “You’re coming in too damned fast.”

The rulebook would have suggested limited direct action from a fixed light in conditions like this: maintain the beam, provide accurate information, relay coordinates. Do not place yourself at unnecessary risk. Do not attempt small craft launch in conditions exceeding…

On the shelf in the service room below, his father’s wrench lay in its box. On the wall by the door hung his old oilskins, long since replaced by a newer set with reflective strips. In the harbor, at the base of the cliff path, was the station’s battered aluminum skiff, tied for calm-weather trips, never meant for a night like this.

But there was also the fog bell.

It had hung once from a timber framework near the foot of the cliff, a great iron mouth that had boomed in pea-soup nights
